questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is classification, and give two reasons why animals are classified?
questions.a: Classification is the grouping of living things according to their similarities and differences. Reasons: it makes study easier and it helps us identify animals and know how to care for them.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between vertebrates and invertebrates.
questions.a: Vertebrates have a backbone; invertebrates do not.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the five classes of vertebrates and one example of each.
questions.a: Mammals — cow; birds — hen; reptiles — lizard; fish — tilapia; amphibians — frog.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which two classes of vertebrates are warm-blooded?
questions.a: Mammals and birds.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four characteristics of mammals.
questions.a: Any four of: body covered with hair or fur; have mammary glands and feed young on milk; give birth to live young; breathe using lungs; are warm-blooded; have external ears.
accepted: have mammary glands and feed young on milk

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four characteristics of birds.
questions.a: Any four of: body covered with feathers; have a beak; have two wings and two legs; lay eggs with hard shells; are warm-blooded; have light hollow bones.
accepted: have two wings and two legs

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three differences between reptiles and amphibians.
questions.a: Reptiles: dry scaly skin, live on land (or water) and breathe with lungs all their life, lay leathery eggs on land. Amphibians: moist smooth skin, live both in water and on land, young breathe with gills and adults with lungs and skin, lay eggs in water. (Any three pairs.)

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: How do fish breathe, and how do they move in water?
questions.a: Fish breathe using gills, and they move using fins and a tail.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three main groups of invertebrates.
questions.a: Arthropods, molluscs and worms.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the four groups of arthropods and give one example of each.
questions.a: Insects — housefly; arachnids — spider; myriapods — millipede; crustaceans — crab.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three differences between insects and arachnids.
questions.a: Insects have 6 legs, arachnids have 8; insects have 3 body parts, arachnids 2; most insects have wings and antennae, arachnids have neither.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between a millipede and a centipede.
questions.a: A millipede has two pairs of legs on each body segment and rolls up when touched; a centipede has one pair per segment and is a fast-moving hunter with poison claws.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why is a bat classified as a mammal and not a bird?
questions.a: Because it has hair on its body, mammary glands and gives birth to live young which it feeds on milk — even though it flies, it has no feathers or beak.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five ways of caring for animals.
questions.a: Any five of: give clean food and water; provide clean dry shelter; treat and vaccinate them; handle them gently; protect them from thieves and wild animals; do not poach; protect their habitats.
accepted: protect them from thieves and wild animals

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five uses of animals to human beings.
questions.a: Any five of: food such as meat, milk, eggs and honey; hides and skins; manure; transport and work; money and employment; tourism; pest control; pollination; company from pets.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is sound, and how is it produced?
questions.a: Sound is a form of energy produced when objects vibrate.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any three natural and three artificial sources of sound.
questions.a: Natural: thunder, wind, animal calls (also flowing water, the human voice). Artificial: a drum, a radio, a bell (also vehicles and machines).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between pitch and volume.
questions.a: Pitch is how high or low a sound is and depends on frequency; volume is how loud or soft a sound is and depends on the size of the vibration.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is frequency, and how does it affect pitch?
questions.a: Frequency is the number of vibrations in one second. The higher the frequency, the higher the pitch.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest, and why?
questions.a: In a solid, because its particles are packed closely together and pass the vibrations on quickly.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum?
questions.a: Because a vacuum has no particles (no medium) to carry the vibrations.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe one experiment that shows sound travels through solids.
questions.a: Place your ear flat on a desk while a friend scratches or taps the far end of the desk. The sound heard through the wood is louder and clearer than through the air, showing that solids carry sound well.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is an echo, and where can it be heard?
questions.a: An echo is a sound heard again after bouncing off a hard surface. It can be heard in valleys, near cliffs, in empty halls and near high walls.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three main parts of the human ear.
questions.a: The outer ear, middle ear and inner ear.
accepted: The outer ear, middle ear and inner ear.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three small bones of the middle ear.
questions.a: The hammer, anvil and stirrup.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: State the work of: the pinna, the ear drum, the cochlea, the auditory nerve.
questions.a: Pinna — collects sound and directs it into the ear canal; ear drum — vibrates when sound hits it; cochlea — changes vibrations into nerve messages; auditory nerve — carries the messages to the brain.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which part of the ear keeps the body in balance?
questions.a: The semi-circular canals.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four diseases or disorders of the ear.
questions.a: Any four of: deafness, otitis media (ear infection), a perforated ear drum, ear wax blockage, foreign bodies in the ear, boils in the ear canal.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five ways of caring for the ear.
questions.a: Any five of: never put sharp objects in the ear; clean only the outer ear with a damp cloth; avoid very loud noise and loud earphones; treat infections early; do not slap anyone on the ear; protect ears from cold; go for check-ups.
accepted: never put sharp objects in the ear
clean only the outer ear with a damp cloth
avoid very loud noise and loud earphones
do not slap anyone on the ear

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three types of musical instruments and give one example of each.
questions.a: String — guitar or adungu; wind — flute or whistle; percussion — drum or xylophone.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three parts of the circulatory system.
questions.a: The heart, the blood vessels and the blood.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Where is the heart found, and what protects it?
questions.a: In the chest, slightly to the left, protected by the ribs (and the breastbone).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the four chambers of the heart and state the work of each.
questions.a: Right atrium — receives blood without oxygen from the body; right ventricle — pumps it to the lungs; left atrium — receives blood with oxygen from the lungs; left ventricle — pumps it to the whole body.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why does the left ventricle have the thickest wall?
questions.a: Because it pumps blood to the whole body, which needs much greater force than pumping to the lungs.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is the work of the valves in the heart?
questions.a: They stop blood from flowing backwards.
accepted: They stop blood from flowing backwards.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three types of blood vessels and give one difference between arteries and veins.
questions.a: Arteries, veins and capillaries. Arteries carry blood away from the heart with thick elastic walls at high pressure, while veins carry blood back to the heart, have thinner walls and contain valves.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Which artery carries blood without oxygen, and which vein carries blood with oxygen?
questions.a: The pulmonary artery carries blood without oxygen; the pulmonary vein carries blood with oxygen.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the four parts of blood and give the work of each.
questions.a: Plasma — carries food, water, salts and waste; red blood cells — carry oxygen; white blood cells — fight germs; platelets — help the blood to clot.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the four blood groups.
questions.a: A, B, AB and O.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four functions of blood.
questions.a: Any four of: transporting oxygen; transporting food and water; carrying waste to the excretory organs; fighting germs; clotting to stop bleeding; spreading heat round the body.
accepted: carrying waste to the excretory organs

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four diseases or disorders of the circulatory system.
questions.a: Any four of: anaemia, sickle cell disease, leukaemia, high blood pressure, heart attack, haemophilia, varicose veins.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three ways in which HIV can be spread through blood, and three ways of preventing this.
questions.a: Spread: transfusion of untested blood; sharing needles or syringes; sharing razor blades or other skin-cutting instruments (also mother to child). Prevention: use only screened blood; use sterile single-use needles; never share razor blades or sharp instruments (and mothers who are HIV positive should follow medical advice).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five ways of increasing the volume of blood in the body.
questions.a: Any five of: eat iron-rich foods such as dodo, nakati, liver, beans and meat; eat fruits rich in vitamin C; deworm regularly; sleep under a mosquito net; treat wounds and bleeding quickly; exercise; rest well; have a transfusion of screened blood in serious cases.
accepted: eat iron-rich foods such as dodo
eat fruits rich in vitamin C
have a transfusion of screened blood in serious cases

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why should blood for transfusion be tested first?
questions.a: To make sure it is the right blood group for the patient and that it is free from germs and infections such as HIV, hepatitis and syphilis, so that the transfusion helps instead of harming.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Trace the path of blood from the body back to the body, naming the chambers and the lungs.
questions.a: Body → right atrium → right ventricle → lungs (to get oxygen) → left atrium → left ventricle → back to the body.

topics.title: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: What is alcoholism? Who is an alcoholic?
questions.a: Alcoholism is the condition of being unable to stop taking alcohol — addiction to alcohol. An alcoholic is a person who is addicted to alcohol.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Give any four effects of alcoholism on the individual.
questions.a: Any four of: damage to the liver, stomach and brain; loss of memory and poor judgement; accidents and injuries; loss of job and poverty; poor health, malnutrition and early death.
accepted: loss of memory and poor judgement

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Give any three effects of alcoholism on the family and three on the community.
questions.a: Family: money wasted instead of buying food and paying fees; quarrels and violence; children dropping out of school; neglect of the family. Community: crime and insecurity; road accidents; loss of a productive workforce; extra burden on hospitals and police. (Any three each.)

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Name any three harmful substances found in tobacco smoke and what each does.
questions.a: Nicotine — causes addiction; tar — causes cancer; carbon monoxide — reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Give the difference between active and passive smoking.
questions.a: Active smoking is smoking a cigarette yourself; passive smoking is breathing in the smoke of somebody else who is smoking.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Why is passive smoking dangerous, especially for children and pregnant mothers?
questions.a: Because passive smokers breathe the same harmful substances and suffer the same diseases, and children's lungs and unborn babies are still developing, so the harm is greater — it can cause coughs, chest infections, poor growth and low birth weight.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Give any four effects of smoking on a person's health.
questions.a: Any four of: lung cancer; chronic cough and bronchitis; tuberculosis; heart disease; stained teeth and bad breath; poor appetite; addiction.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: What are essential drugs? Give any four examples.
questions.a: Essential drugs are the medicines a community most needs and which should always be available at a health centre. Examples: ORS, paracetamol, anti-malarial tablets, antibiotics, deworming tablets, vaccines (any four).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Give any four characteristics of good drugs.
questions.a: Any four of: within the expiry date; properly sealed and labelled; from a licensed health centre or pharmacy; with the correct name, dose and instructions; not discoloured, crushed or damp.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Give any five rules for storing drugs safely in a home.
questions.a: Any five of: keep them in a cool, dry, dark place; keep them in the original labelled container; close them tightly; keep them out of reach of children, preferably locked; do not store them with food or paraffin; check the expiry date; destroy or return expired drugs safely.
accepted: keep them in the original labelled container
keep them out of reach of children
do not store them with food

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Give the difference between drug abuse and drug misuse, with one example of each.
questions.a: Drug abuse is using a drug for a purpose it was not meant for, for example sniffing petrol. Drug misuse is using a proper medicine wrongly, for example taking the wrong dose or using somebody else's prescription.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: What is drug dependence?
questions.a: Drug dependence is when the body or the mind can no longer do without the drug, so the person suffers when he or she stops taking it.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Name any four commonly abused substances.
questions.a: Any four of: alcohol, tobacco, marijuana (njaga), khat (mairungi), petrol or glue fumes, cocaine, heroin, wrongly used sleeping tablets.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Give any five factors that lead young people into alcoholism, smoking or drug abuse.
questions.a: Any five of: peer pressure; curiosity; idleness and too much free time; copying parents or film and music stars; advertising; frustration and family problems; easy availability; lack of guidance.
accepted: idleness and too much free time

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Alcohol, Smoking and Drugs in Society
questions.q: Name any five life skills that help a young person to refuse drugs, and explain one of them.
questions.a: Any five of: assertiveness, peer pressure resistance, decision-making, critical thinking, self-esteem, coping with stress, effective communication, using free time well. Assertiveness, for example, is the ability to say NO firmly and to repeat it without fear or apology, and to walk away from the situation.
accepted: is the ability to say NO firmly and to repeat it without fear
and to walk away from the situation

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between flowering and non-flowering plants, with two examples of each.
questions.a: Flowering plants produce flowers and seeds, for example maize and mango; non-flowering plants do not produce flowers, for example ferns and pine.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the three groups of non-flowering plants and give one example of each.
questions.a: Spore-bearing plants — fern; conifers — pine; algae — spirogyra (or seaweed).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three differences between legumes and cereals.
questions.a: Legumes: seeds in pods, two seed leaves, root nodules that add nitrogen, rich in protein. Cereals: grasses grown for grain, one seed leaf, fibrous roots, rich in carbohydrates. (Any three pairs.)

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why is planting legumes good for the soil?
questions.a: Because their root nodules contain bacteria that add nitrogen to the soil, making it fertile again for the next crop.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the male and the female parts of a flower and state the work of each.
questions.a: The stamen (anther and filament) is the male part and makes pollen; the pistil (stigma, style and ovary) is the female part and receives pollen and holds the ovules.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is pollination, and what happens to the ovary after fertilisation?
questions.a: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma. After fertilisation the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules become seeds.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is seed dispersal, and give any four reasons why it is necessary?
questions.a: Seed dispersal is the scattering of seeds away from the parent plant. Reasons: to avoid overcrowding; to reduce competition for water, light and food; to spread the plant to new areas; to reduce the spread of pests and diseases (any four).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the five agents of seed dispersal.
questions.a: Wind, water, animals (and birds), explosive mechanism, and people.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the features of a seed dispersed by wind and one dispersed by animals.
questions.a: Wind: the seed is light and has wings, hairs or a parachute. Animals: the fruit is sweet and fleshy so it is eaten, or the seed has hooks that stick to fur and clothes.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is plant propagation? Name its two types.
questions.a: Plant propagation is the way new plants are produced from old ones. Its two types are sexual (by seeds) and vegetative (asexual).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six methods of vegetative propagation, with one example of each.
questions.a: Any six: cuttings — cassava; suckers — banana; tubers — Irish potato; bulbs — onion; rhizomes — ginger; runners — grass; grafting — mango; layering — guava.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
questions.a: Advantages: the new plant is exactly like the parent and it matures faster. Disadvantages: diseases are passed on easily and there is no variety among the plants.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six economic values of plants.
questions.a: Any six of: food; cash crops and employment; timber and poles; firewood and charcoal; medicine; raw materials for industries; fodder for animals; shade and windbreaks; protection of the environment and supply of oxygen; tourism.
accepted: protection of the environment and supply of oxygen

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why do farmers plant beans in a garden where maize was grown the season before?
questions.a: Because the beans are a legume whose root nodules add nitrogen to the soil, restoring the fertility that the maize used up. This is crop rotation.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give one plant grown from each of: cuttings, suckers, bulbs, rhizomes, tubers.
questions.a: Cuttings — cassava; suckers — banana; bulbs — onion; rhizomes — ginger; tubers — Irish potato (or sweet potato).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name the four types of cattle and what each is kept for.
questions.a: Dairy — milk; beef — meat; dual-purpose — both milk and meat; work (draught) — ploughing and pulling carts.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between indigenous and exotic breeds, with two examples of each.
questions.a: Indigenous breeds have always been in the country, for example Ankole long-horned and Zebu; exotic breeds were brought from other countries, for example Friesian and Jersey.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give two advantages of indigenous breeds and two of exotic breeds.
questions.a: Indigenous: resist diseases and heat, and can walk long distances for pasture and water. Exotic: give much more milk or meat, and mature faster.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six external features of a cow.
questions.a: Any six of: horns, eyes, ears, muzzle, dewlap, hump, udder with teats, tail, hooves, hide, back, flank.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three differences between a cow and a bull.
questions.a: A cow has an udder with four teats while a bull has none; a bull has a larger head and thicker neck and shoulders; a bull is usually stronger and fiercer, while the cow is gentler and produces milk.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Define: heifer, steer, calf.
questions.a: Heifer — a young female that has not yet calved; steer (ox) — a castrated male; calf — the young one of cattle.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four methods of grazing cattle.
questions.a: Any four of: free range, paddocking, tethering, zero grazing, strip grazing.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three advantages of zero grazing.
questions.a: Any three of: it suits a small piece of land; the milk and the animal stay clean; manure is easily collected; the animal uses less energy so it gives more milk; it is easy to control diseases and feeding.
accepted: it suits a small piece of land
the milk and the animal stay clean
the animal uses less energy so it gives more milk
it is easy to control diseases and feeding

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any five feeds given to cattle.
questions.a: Any five of: pasture grasses, fodder such as elephant grass, legumes such as calliandra, crop residues, concentrates such as dairy meal, mineral salt licks, and clean water.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five qualities of a good cattle shed.
questions.a: Any five of: spacious, dry, well ventilated, easy to clean, with a concrete or sloping floor, a good roof, feeding and watering places, a calf pen, a milking area and a crush.
accepted: a milking area and a crush

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is the gestation period of a cow? What is calving?
questions.a: The gestation period is about nine months (280 days). Calving is the act of giving birth to a calf.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is colostrum, and why must the calf get it?
questions.a: Colostrum is the first thick yellow milk produced after calving. The calf must get it because it is rich in antibodies that protect it from disease, and in nutrients for a good start.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any three advantages of artificial insemination.
questions.a: Any three of: a farmer can use a very good bull without keeping one; it prevents diseases spread by mating; one bull can serve very many cows; it improves the breed quickly; it is cheaper than keeping a bull.
accepted: a farmer can use a very good bull without keeping one
it prevents diseases spread by mating
one bull can serve very many cows
it is cheaper than keeping a bull

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six rules of clean milking.
questions.a: Any six of: milk at the same time daily; wash hands and the udder with clean warm water and dry them; use clean dry metal containers; use the full-hand method; milk quickly and completely; keep the shed clean; sieve and cool the milk at once; a sick person or sick cow must not supply milk.
accepted: milk at the same time daily
wash hands and the udder with clean warm water and dry them
sieve and cool the milk at once
sick cow must not supply milk

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any five milk products.
questions.a: Any five of: ghee, butter, yoghurt, cheese, sour milk, cream, powdered milk, ice cream.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four cattle pests and the harm each causes.
questions.a: Any four: ticks — suck blood and spread East Coast fever; tsetse flies — spread nagana; worms — cause anaemia and poor growth; lice and mites — cause irritation and wounds.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four cattle diseases and one way of controlling each.
questions.a: Any four, for example: foot and mouth disease — vaccination and quarantine; East Coast fever — spraying or dipping against ticks; nagana — control tsetse flies and clear bush; mastitis — clean milking and treatment; anthrax — vaccination and never opening the carcass.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five practices that harm cattle.
questions.a: Any five of: beating and overworking; rough or over-milking; tethering with no shade or water; overstocking and overgrazing; using dirty instruments for dehorning or castration; burning pasture; using wrong or expired drugs.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six steps in starting a livestock farm.
questions.a: Any six of: choose a suitable site; decide the type of cattle and the system; get capital and plan; prepare land, pasture and fencing; build the shed and crush; buy healthy stock; arrange feeds and water; register with the veterinary officer; keep records; find a market.
accepted: decide the type of cattle and the system

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why should a farmer keep records on a cattle farm?
questions.a: Because records show which cows produce most milk, when each was served and is due to calve, what treatment was given, and how much money came in and went out — so the farmer can plan, breed better animals and know whether the farm is making a profit.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is a resource? Give three living and three non-living resources.
questions.a: A resource is anything in the environment that people use to satisfy their needs. Living: plants, animals, fish (also birds, insects, people). Non-living: soil, water, air (also minerals, sunlight, rocks).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why are human beings called a resource?
questions.a: Because people provide labour, skills, ideas and leadership that are needed to use all the other resources and to develop the country.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is harvesting? Give the way each of these is harvested: fish, timber, salt, minerals.
questions.a: Harvesting is collecting a resource from the environment for use. Fish — nets, hooks and traps; timber — felling trees and sawing; salt — evaporating water from salt lakes such as Katwe; minerals — mining, quarrying, drilling or panning.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five good harvesting practices.
questions.a: Any five of: take only what is needed; use the right tools and methods; leave young plants, fish and animals to grow; avoid poison, explosives and undersized nets; replant after cutting trees; avoid harvesting in the breeding season; store the harvest well.
accepted: use the right tools and methods
avoid harvesting in the breeding season

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four uses of water and four uses of soil.
questions.a: Water: drinking, cooking and washing, irrigation, fishing, transport, hydro-electric power (any four). Soil: growing crops, making bricks, making pots, building, holding plant roots (any four).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between renewable and non-renewable resources.
questions.a: Renewable resources can be replaced or never run out, such as sunlight and wind; non-renewable resources get used up and cannot be replaced, such as gold and petroleum.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Classify these as renewable or non-renewable: sunlight, copper, wind, petroleum, forests.
questions.a: Renewable: sunlight, wind, forests. Non-renewable: copper, petroleum.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why are plants and animals renewable only under certain conditions?
questions.a: Because they can only replace themselves if they are given time and conditions to reproduce. If people cut trees or catch fish faster than they can reproduce, they are used up completely and may become extinct.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is meant by depletion of a resource? Give one example.
questions.a: Depletion is using up a resource until very little is left, for example over-fishing on a lake until the fish stocks nearly disappear (or over-cutting of forests).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What does it mean when an animal species is said to be extinct?
questions.a: It means the species no longer exists anywhere — every member of it has died and it can never be brought back.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is conservation?
questions.a: Conservation is protecting and using resources carefully so that they are not destroyed or used up.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five ways of conserving soil.
questions.a: Any five of: mulching, terracing, contour ploughing, crop rotation, applying manure, planting cover crops, controlled grazing, planting trees.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four ways of conserving water.
questions.a: Any four of: harvesting rain water, protecting springs and wetlands, avoiding pollution, closing taps, careful irrigation, repairing leaking pipes.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four ways of conserving forests and four ways of protecting wild animals and fish.
questions.a: Forests: afforestation, reafforestation, agroforestry, energy-saving stoves, forest reserves (any four). Animals and fish: game parks and sanctuaries, laws against poaching, closed fishing seasons, correct net sizes, fish farming (any four).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five reasons why resources must be conserved.
questions.a: Any five of: so that resources last for future generations; to keep the environment healthy; to keep soil fertile and rainfall reliable; to protect wildlife and tourism; to avoid famine and poverty; to prevent conflicts over scarce resources.
accepted: so that resources last for future generations
to keep soil fertile and rainfall reliable
to prevent conflicts over scarce resources

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between breathing and respiration.
questions.a: Breathing is simply taking in and giving out air, while respiration is the process by which the body breaks down food to release energy inside the cells.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any six organs of the respiratory system.
questions.a: Any six of: nose, pharynx, epiglottis, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, lungs, diaphragm.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: State the work of: the nose, the epiglottis, the trachea, the alveoli, the diaphragm.
questions.a: Nose — takes in air and filters, warms and moistens it; epiglottis — closes the windpipe when swallowing; trachea — carries air to the lungs; alveoli — where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves; diaphragm — the muscle that flattens and relaxes to help breathing.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Trace the path taken by air from outside the body to the blood.
questions.a: Nose → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli → blood.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why is it better to breathe through the nose than through the mouth?
questions.a: Because the nose has hairs and mucus that trap dust and germs, and it warms and moistens the air before it reaches the lungs; the mouth does none of these.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe what happens to the diaphragm and the ribs when a person breathes in.
questions.a: The diaphragm flattens and moves downwards, the ribs move upwards and outwards, the chest cavity increases in size and air rushes into the lungs.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give three differences between inhaled and exhaled air.
questions.a: Any three of: inhaled air has more oxygen (21% against 16%); exhaled air has much more carbon dioxide (about 4% against 0.03%); exhaled air has more water vapour; exhaled air is warmer.
accepted: inhaled air has more oxygen (21% against 16%)
exhaled air has much more carbon dioxide (about 4% against 0.03%)
exhaled air has more water vapour

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe one experiment that shows exhaled air contains carbon dioxide.
questions.a: Breathe out through a straw into lime water. The lime water turns milky, showing that carbon dioxide is present. (Comparing with air blown in by a pump shows the difference.)

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Describe one experiment that shows exhaled air contains water vapour.
questions.a: Breathe onto a cold mirror or glass. Tiny drops of water form on it, showing that exhaled air contains water vapour.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Write the word equation for respiration.
questions.a: Food (glucose) + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four uses of the energy released during respiration.
questions.a: Any four of: movement and work; growth and repair of the body; keeping the body warm; the beating of the heart and the working of other organs; thinking; digestion.
accepted: growth and repair of the body
the beating of the heart and the working of other organs

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any five diseases of the respiratory system.
questions.a: Any five of: tuberculosis, pneumonia, bronchitis, asthma, the common cold and flu, whooping cough, lung cancer, diphtheria.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the cause and two signs of tuberculosis.
questions.a: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria spread through coughing and sneezing by an infected person. Signs: a cough lasting more than two weeks, chest pain, weight loss, night sweats, fever (any two).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six ways of keeping the respiratory system healthy.
questions.a: Any six of: do not smoke and avoid other people's smoke; keep rooms well ventilated; avoid dust and cooking smoke; cover the mouth when coughing; immunise children; eat a balanced diet; exercise regularly; breathe through the nose; avoid overcrowded rooms; treat coughs and colds early; plant trees.
accepted: do not smoke and avoid other people's smoke

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: How does the circulatory system help the respiratory system?
questions.a: The blood, especially the red blood cells, carries oxygen from the alveoli to every cell of the body, and carries the waste carbon dioxide back to the lungs to be breathed out. Without the circulatory system, the oxygen would never reach the cells.

topics.title: Science at Home and in Our Community

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Give the difference between clean water and safe water.
questions.a: Clean water has no dirt that you can see, while safe water is free from germs and harmful substances and can be drunk without causing disease. Water can look clean and still be unsafe.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Name any five impurities found in water and where each comes from.
questions.a: Any five, for example: human wastes — from poor latrines and open defecation; animal wastes — from animals at the water source; fertilisers and pesticides — from gardens; oils and chemicals — from factories and garages; silt and leaves — washed in by rain; rubbish and polythene — from homes.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Name any four diseases caused by drinking unsafe water.
questions.a: Any four of: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, diarrhoea, bilharzia, worms, hepatitis.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Name five methods of making water safe for drinking.
questions.a: Boiling, filtering, treating with chemicals, distilling and decanting (also solar disinfection).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Describe how water is made safe by decanting.
questions.a: The dirty water is left to stand undisturbed in a container until the heavy particles settle at the bottom. The clear water on top is then poured off carefully into another clean container, leaving the sediment behind.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Why is boiling the commonest method used in homes?
questions.a: Because it is cheap and easy — every home has a fire — and it kills the germs that cause disease, needing no special chemicals or equipment.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Which method gives the purest water, and why?
questions.a: Distillation, because boiling turns the water into steam, leaving germs, salts and other dissolved substances behind; the steam is then cooled back into very pure water.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Give the correct order of treating very dirty water and say why that order is used.
questions.a: First decant or filter to remove the dirt you can see, then boil or treat to kill the germs, then store in a clean covered container. Filtering first is important because dirt and solid matter can protect germs from the treatment and make chemicals less effective.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Give any four rules for storing drinking water safely.
questions.a: Any four of: use a clean covered container; use a tap or long-handled cup so hands do not enter; never mix treated with untreated water; clean the container regularly; keep it away from animals and small children.
accepted: long-handled cup so hands do not enter
never mix treated with untreated water
keep it away from animals and small children

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Give any five ways of protecting a water source.
questions.a: Any five of: fence the source; build a drainage channel; keep latrines at least 30 m away and downhill; do not wash clothes or bathe at the source; do not water animals there; do not dig or farm next to it; plant grass around it.
accepted: keep latrines at least 30 m away and downhill

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Name any four plant materials used to make salt.
questions.a: Any four of: dry banana peelings, banana stems, bean stalks, millet stalks, papyrus reeds, water-lily plants.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Describe, in steps, how salt is made from plant materials.
questions.a: Dry the plant material → burn it into ash → put the ash in a container or funnel-shaped basket lined with grass → pour clean water slowly through the ash (leaching) → collect the filtrate → boil it until all the water evaporates → the solid salt is left behind.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Which three science processes are shown when making salt from plants?
questions.a: Dissolving, filtering and evaporation.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Give any six steps followed when washing clothes at home.
questions.a: Any six of: sort the clothes; empty the pockets and shake off dust; soak them in soapy water; wash by rubbing or brushing the dirty parts; rinse two or three times; hang them in the sun to dry; iron them; fold and store them cleanly.
accepted: empty the pockets and shake off dust
hang them in the sun to dry

questions.subject: SCI
questions.topic: Science at Home and in Our Community
questions.q: Give any four reasons why clothes should be washed and ironed.
questions.a: Any four of: to remove dirt, sweat and bad smell; to kill germs and prevent skin diseases; to kill jiggers and lice by ironing; to make the clothes last longer; to look smart and keep self-respect.
accepted: to kill germs and prevent skin diseases
to kill jiggers and lice by ironing
to make the clothes last longer
to look smart and keep self-respect

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is first aid, and who is a first aider?
questions.a: First aid is the immediate help given to an injured or suddenly sick person before a health worker arrives or before the person reaches hospital. A first aider is the person who gives it.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four aims of first aid.
questions.a: Any four of: to save life; to prevent the injury from getting worse; to relieve pain; to promote recovery; to get the person quickly to proper medical care.
accepted: to prevent the injury from getting worse
to get the person quickly to proper medical care

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five qualities of a good first aider.
questions.a: Any five of: calm and confident; quick but careful; clean; kind and comforting; observant; knows his or her limits; sends for help early.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any eight items found in a first-aid kit.
questions.a: Any eight of: cotton wool, bandages, gauze, plaster, scissors, antiseptic, gloves, a thermometer, safety pins, clean water, a torch, ORS, a splint, a notebook and pen.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between a burn and a scald, with one cause of each.
questions.a: A burn is caused by dry heat, for example fire or a hot iron; a scald is caused by moist heat, for example hot water or steam.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the steps of first aid for a burn.
questions.a: Remove the person from the source of heat (switching off electricity if needed) → cool the part with clean cool water for 10–20 minutes → remove tight clothing near the burn before swelling → cover with a clean dry non-fluffy cloth → give fluids if the person is fully awake → take them to a health centre if the burn is large, deep or on the face or hands.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four things that should never be put on a burn.
questions.a: Any four of: cow dung, engine oil, paraffin, mud, butter, toothpaste, ash, ice.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four ways of preventing burns and scalds at home.
questions.a: Any four of: keep children away from the fireplace and kitchen; turn saucepan handles inwards; put out fires properly; lock away paraffin, petrol and matches; do not overload sockets; put out candles before sleeping; keep hot drinks away from table edges.
accepted: keep children away from the fireplace and kitchen
keep hot drinks away from table edges

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is fever, and what is the normal body temperature?
questions.a: Fever is a body temperature higher than normal. The normal body temperature is about 37 °C.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the first aid for a child with a high fever.
questions.a: Move the child to a cool airy place → remove heavy clothing → sponge with lukewarm water → give plenty of fluids → give the correct dose of fever medicine if available → take the child for a malaria test and treatment quickly.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What are convulsions? Give three causes.
questions.a: Convulsions are sudden uncontrollable jerking of the body. Causes: very high fever in a child, epilepsy, cerebral malaria or meningitis (any three).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five steps of first aid for a person having convulsions, and two things you must not do.
questions.a: Do: stay calm and call for help; lay the person on the floor on their side away from fire, water and sharp objects; loosen tight clothing; put something soft under the head; after the fit, keep them on their side and take them to a health centre. Do not: put anything in the mouth; hold the person down or pour cold water on them.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the first aid for a person who has nearly drowned, and say why a weak swimmer should not jump in.
questions.a: Reach out to the person with a stick, rope or floating object; once out, lay them on their side so water drains; check breathing; keep them warm; if they are not breathing, give rescue breathing if trained and keep calling for help; take them to hospital. A weak swimmer should not jump in because the drowning person panics and clings, and both can drown.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five ways of preventing drowning.
questions.a: Any five of: learn to swim; never swim alone or in flooded rivers; do not overload boats and wear life jackets; never play near wells or tanks; cover wells and tanks; watch small children near any water; do not swim after a heavy meal or in a storm.
accepted: do not overload boats and wear life jackets
watch small children near any water
do not swim after a heavy meal

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is fainting? Give three causes and the first aid given.
questions.a: Fainting is a short loss of consciousness caused by too little blood reaching the brain. Causes: standing too long in the sun, hunger, tiredness, shock or fear (any three). First aid: lay the person flat in a cool airy place, raise the legs, loosen tight clothing, allow fresh air, sponge the face, and give water when they wake.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why is a person who has fainted made to lie down with the legs raised?
questions.a: Because raising the legs helps blood flow back to the brain, which is what was lacking, so the person recovers quickly.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is a foreign body? Give the first aid for an insect in the ear and for dust in the eye.
questions.a: A foreign body is anything that enters the body where it does not belong. Insect in the ear: pour a little clean cooking oil or warm water to float it out, then see a health worker if it remains. Dust in the eye: do not rub; wash it out with clean water, or lift the upper eyelid over the lower one.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What should be done for a child who has swallowed paraffin, and what must never be done?
questions.a: The child should be taken to hospital immediately, carrying the container if possible, and kept calm and on their side. Never make the child vomit, because paraffin coming back up can enter the lungs and cause serious damage.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the first aid for a person choking on food.
questions.a: Encourage the person to cough; bend a child forward and give firm back blows between the shoulder blades; keep checking the mouth and remove anything you can see easily; call for help at once if the object does not come out.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why should a person who has nearly drowned be taken to hospital even if they look well?
questions.a: Because water that entered the lungs can cause breathing problems and infection several hours later, so the person must be checked by a health worker even if they seem to have recovered.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is sanitation?
questions.a: Sanitation is keeping the surroundings clean and disposing of human waste and rubbish safely so that people stay healthy.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any five diseases caused by poor sanitation.
questions.a: Any five of: cholera, typhoid, dysentery, diarrhoea, worms, bilharzia, hepatitis, jiggers.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the full meaning of VIP latrine.
questions.a: Ventilated Improved Pit latrine.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name three special features of a VIP latrine and explain how it removes smell.
questions.a: Features: a vent pipe from the pit to above the roof, a fly screen at the top of the pipe, and a dark interior with an uncovered squat hole. The sun heats the vent pipe so the air inside rises and carries the smell out, while fresh air enters through the door.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: How does a VIP latrine control flies?
questions.a: Flies in the dark pit fly towards the light at the top of the vent pipe and are trapped by the fly screen, where they die.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of an ordinary pit latrine.
questions.a: Advantage: it is cheap and easy to build with local materials and needs no water. Disadvantage: it smells and attracts flies (it also fills up and must be replaced).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is an Ecosan toilet, and what is added after each use?
questions.a: An Ecosan (ecological sanitation) toilet is one that separates urine from faeces and turns the waste into manure. Ash or dry soil is added after each use.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any three advantages of an Ecosan toilet.
questions.a: Any three of: it provides manure; it suits rocky, sandy, waterlogged or crowded areas; it does not pollute ground water; there is no smell when ash is used; no deep pit has to be dug.
accepted: it does not pollute ground water
there is no smell when ash is used
no deep pit has to be dug

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: In what kind of areas is an Ecosan toilet especially useful, and why?
questions.a: In rocky, sandy, waterlogged or very crowded areas, because a deep pit cannot be dug safely there and a pit would collapse or pollute the ground water.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is a potty, and how should it be used and cleaned?
questions.a: A potty is a small portable container used by babies and small children who cannot use the latrine. It must be emptied into the latrine immediately, washed with clean water and soap, and dried in the sun — never emptied in the compound.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is a water closet? Give two advantages and two disadvantages.
questions.a: A water closet is a flush toilet with a cistern and a water seal that carries waste to a septic tank or sewer. Advantages: it is clean and has no smell; it is comfortable and free from flies. Disadvantages: it needs plenty of piped water; it is expensive and blocks easily.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six importances of using a toilet or latrine.
questions.a: Any six of: it prevents diseases such as cholera and worms; it keeps the compound and gardens free of human waste; it controls flies and bad smells; it protects water sources; it gives privacy and dignity; it keeps the home clean; it is required by public health law.
accepted: it prevents diseases such as cholera and worms
it keeps the compound and gardens free of human waste
it controls flies and bad smells
it is required by public health law

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Explain how disease travels from faeces to the mouth, and how using a latrine breaks the path.
questions.a: Faeces left in the open are carried to food and the mouth by flies, fingers, food, fluids and fields — the "five Fs". Using a latrine keeps the faeces sealed in a pit so flies and feet cannot carry them, and washing hands with soap removes what is on the fingers, so the path is broken.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six rules for the proper use of a latrine.
questions.a: Any six of: use the latrine every time; aim into the hole and keep the slab clean; cover the hole after use in an ordinary latrine; put used paper in the pit; add ash in an Ecosan toilet; flush a water closet; wash hands with soap afterwards; teach children to use the potty properly.
accepted: aim into the hole and keep the slab clean
cover the hole after use in an ordinary latrine
put used paper in the pit
add ash in an Ecosan toilet
teach children to use the potty properly

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six ways of maintaining a latrine.
questions.a: Any six of: sweep and scrub the floor and slab daily; use water or disinfectant; keep soap and water at the door; repair cracks, doors and roofs; keep the vent screen in good order; keep the door closed; do not throw rubbish into the pit; plant grass around it; dig a new pit when it is nearly full.
accepted: sweep and scrub the floor and slab daily
keep soap and water at the door
keep the vent screen in good order
do not throw rubbish into the pit
dig a new pit when it is nearly full

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why should rubbish and polythene never be thrown into a pit latrine?
questions.a: Because they do not rot, so they fill the pit quickly and shorten its life, and in a flush toilet they cause blockages.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Where should a latrine be sited in relation to a water source and the house?
questions.a: At least 30 metres from a water source and downhill from it, and about 6 metres from the house, downwind, on firm well-drained ground.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between a VIP latrine and an ordinary pit latrine in the way the squat hole is treated.
questions.a: In a VIP latrine the squat hole is left uncovered so that air can flow through the pit and up the vent pipe; in an ordinary pit latrine the hole is covered after use to keep out flies and reduce the smell.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Why should hands be washed with soap after using a latrine?
questions.a: Because germs from faeces remain on the fingers, and hands touch food, water and other people. Washing with soap removes those germs and prevents diseases such as diarrhoea, cholera and worms.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What should be done when a pit latrine is nearly full?
questions.a: It should be closed and covered with soil and a new pit dug elsewhere; the slab can be moved to the new pit, and the old site should be marked and, in time, planted with trees.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between growth and development.
questions.a: Growth is an increase in the size and weight of the body, while development is the change that makes the body able to do more, such as walking, talking and reproducing.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is puberty, and at about what age does it begin in girls and in boys?
questions.a: Puberty is the stage at which the reproductive organs become mature and a young person becomes able to produce children. It begins at about 10–14 years in girls and 12–16 years in boys.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is adolescence?
questions.a: Adolescence is the period of change between childhood and adulthood, affecting the body, the mind and the feelings.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four physical changes at puberty in girls and four in boys.
questions.a: Girls: breasts develop; hips widen; menstruation begins; pubic and armpit hair grows (also oily skin, rapid growth). Boys: the voice deepens; the chest and shoulders broaden; wet dreams begin; facial, pubic and armpit hair grows.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four social and emotional changes during adolescence.
questions.a: Any four of: wanting independence; strong peer influence; quick changes of mood; shyness; interest in the opposite sex; wanting privacy; new interest in appearance.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the difference between primary and secondary sex characteristics, with two examples of each.
questions.a: Primary characteristics are the reproductive organs present at birth, for example the testes and the ovaries. Secondary characteristics appear at puberty, for example breasts in girls and a deep voice in boys.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four parts of the male reproductive system and the work of each.
questions.a: Any four: testes — produce sperm cells; scrotum — holds the testes and keeps them cool; sperm duct — carries sperms; urethra — passes semen and urine out; penis — the organ through which semen and urine leave the body.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name any four parts of the female reproductive system and the work of each.
questions.a: Any four: ovaries — produce egg cells; fallopian tubes — carry the egg and are where fertilisation happens; uterus — where the baby develops; cervix — the neck of the uterus; vagina — the passage to the outside.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Where are sperm cells produced, and where are egg cells produced?
questions.a: Sperm cells are produced in the testes; egg cells are produced in the ovaries.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is menstruation, and about how long is the menstrual cycle?
questions.a: Menstruation is the monthly flow of blood and the lining of the uterus through the vagina when the egg has not been fertilised. The cycle is about 28 days.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is fertilisation, and where does it take place?
questions.a: Fertilisation is the joining of a sperm cell and an egg cell. It takes place in the fallopian tube (oviduct).

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give the meaning of conception, zygote and gestation.
questions.a: Conception — the fertilised egg attaching to the wall of the uterus and beginning to grow; zygote — the single cell formed at fertilisation; gestation — the period the baby develops in the womb.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: How long does pregnancy last, and what is the work of the placenta?
questions.a: Pregnancy lasts about nine months (40 weeks). The placenta supplies the baby with food and oxygen from the mother and carries away its waste.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four signs of pregnancy.
questions.a: Any four of: the monthly periods stop; morning sickness; the breasts enlarge; the abdomen grows; tiredness; changes in appetite.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six ways of caring for a pregnant mother.
questions.a: Any six of: attend antenatal clinic early and regularly; eat a balanced diet rich in iron; take the supplements given; sleep under a treated mosquito net; rest and avoid heavy work; avoid alcohol, smoking and self-medication; keep clean; deliver at a health centre with a trained health worker.
accepted: attend antenatal clinic early and regularly
eat a balanced diet rich in iron
sleep under a treated mosquito net
deliver at a health centre with a trained health worker

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any four problems that can occur during pregnancy.
questions.a: Any four of: anaemia, malaria, high blood pressure, miscarriage, bleeding, excessive vomiting, obstructed labour, malnutrition, infections including HIV.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any five effects of teenage pregnancy and four ways of preventing it.
questions.a: Effects (any five): danger to the health and life of the girl and baby; obstructed labour and fistula; low birth weight; dropping out of school; poverty; stigma and rejection; unsafe abortion. Prevention (any four): stay in school; abstain from sex; avoid bad company, alcohol and drugs; refuse gifts and lifts from older people; report abuse to a trusted adult; get correct information from parents and health workers.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Give any six ways of caring for the reproductive organs.
questions.a: Any six of: bathe daily and wash the private parts with clean water; wear clean cotton underwear and change it daily; wipe from front to back; use and change clean sanitary materials; never insert anything into the private parts; avoid harmful traditional practices; treat itching or discharge early; abstain from sex; report anybody who touches you wrongly.
accepted: bathe daily and wash the private parts with clean water
wear clean cotton underwear and change it daily
use and change clean sanitary materials
never insert anything into the private parts
report anybody who touches you wrongly

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: What is family planning? Give any five reasons why it is important.
questions.a: Family planning is deciding how many children to have and when to have them, using acceptable methods. Importance (any five): it protects the mother's health; it gives each child better care and education; it reduces infant and maternal deaths; it helps the family plan its money; it slows very rapid population growth; it allows parents to work and rest.

questions.subject: SCI
questions.q: Name three natural and three artificial methods of family planning, and correct any two myths about family planning.
questions.a: Natural: abstinence, the calendar (rhythm) method, breastfeeding in the early months. Artificial: condoms, pills, injections (also implants, the loop). Myths corrected: "family planning makes a woman permanently barren" — most methods are reversible and fertility returns when they are stopped; "it is only for women" — it is the responsibility of both partners.
